verses.text: On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar, the king's orders were due to take effect. The enemies of the Jews had hoped to overpower them that day, but things were reversed. The Jews overcame those who hated them.

The Jews gathered in their cities throughout King Ahasuerus's provinces to defend themselves against anyone who meant to harm them. No one could stand against them because the people had become afraid of them.
The provincial leaders, local governors, and royal officials all helped the Jews because they were afraid of Mordecai.
Mordecai held a powerful position in the palace, and word about him spread through every province. He was growing more powerful all the time.
The Jews struck down their enemies with the sword, killing and destroying them. They did as they wished with those who hated them.
In the fortress of Susa, the Jews killed five hundred men.
They killed Parshandatha, Dalphon, and Aspatha,
Poratha, Adalia, and Aridatha,
Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai, and Vaizatha,
the ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews. They took none of their property.
The number of people killed in the fortress of Susa was reported to the king that day.

The king told Queen Esther, "The Jews have killed five hundred men in the fortress of Susa, including Haman's ten sons. What must they have done in the rest of the provinces? Now what else are you asking for? I'll grant it. What more do you request? It will be done."
Esther answered, "If it pleases the king, allow the Jews in Susa to act under today's decree tomorrow too, and have the bodies of Haman's ten sons hung on the gallows."
The king gave the order. A decree was issued in Susa, and Haman's ten sons were hung.
The Jews in Susa gathered again on the fourteenth day of Adar and killed three hundred men there, but took none of their property.

The other Jews across the king's provinces gathered to defend themselves and found relief from their enemies. They killed seventy-five thousand of those who hated them, but took none of their property.
This happened on the thirteenth day of Adar. On the fourteenth they rested and made it a day of feasting and joy.
The Jews in Susa gathered on the thirteenth and fourteenth days, then rested on the fifteenth and made it a day of feasting and joy.
That's why Jews who live in villages and unwalled towns celebrate the fourteenth day of Adar as a holiday, feasting, rejoicing, and sending gifts of food to one another.
Mordecai wrote down what had happened and sent letters to the Jews in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, near and far.
He told them to observe the fourteenth and fifteenth days of Adar every year,

because these were the days when the Jews found relief from their enemies. That month their sorrow turned into joy and their mourning into a holiday. They were to mark those days by feasting and celebrating, sending food to one another, and giving gifts to people in need.
The Jews agreed to continue the custom they had begun, just as Mordecai had written to them.
Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted to destroy them and had cast the Pur, meaning the lot, to decide when to wipe them out.
When the king learned of it, he issued a written order that Haman's evil plot against the Jews should fall back on his own head and that he and his sons should be hung on the gallows.
That's why the days are called Purim, from the word Pur. In light of the letter, what they had seen, and what had happened to them,
the Jews took on a lasting obligation for themselves, their descendants, and everyone who joined them. They would observe these two days each year in the way prescribed and at the appointed time.

These days were to be remembered and observed from generation to generation in every family, province, and city. The Jews were to keep celebrating Purim, and their descendants were never to forget it.
Queen Esther daughter of Abihail and Mordecai the Jew wrote with full authority to confirm this second letter about Purim.
Mordecai sent letters with words of peace and truth to all the Jews in the hundred twenty-seven provinces of Ahasuerus's kingdom.

The letters confirmed the appointed dates for Purim, as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther had decreed and as the people had pledged for themselves and their descendants, along with the observances of fasting and mourning.
Esther's command confirmed these practices for Purim, and it was written in the book.
